A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JUREX-4E and retain matching core methods, datasets, and results. Inspection of all pages, including figures, tables, and appendices, supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original human evaluations, similar-charge disambiguation experiments, legal-case retrieval results, and a retrieval case study.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds model and prompting comparisons, a charge-prediction pilot, and an expert–LLM collaboration experiment.

M1.justification: V2 Section 9 introduces a preliminary collaboration procedure: an LLM retrieves statutes and extracts factual keywords, experts validate them, and the LLM produces refined annotations. This is a limited alternative annotation procedure; the original hierarchical expert annotation and retrieval method, including the 70:30 similarity combination, remain substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 Appendix D adds direct charge-prediction evaluation covering unrestricted, multi-charge and multi-defendant cases, extending the reported task scenarios beyond binary charge disambiguation and retrieval. The 155-charge knowledge base, three disambiguation groups, and LeCaRDv2 retrieval coverage are retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds Farui-plus and Qwen comparisons, differently sourced and combined FETs, an in-context-learning variant, and collaborative annotations. GEAR disappears from the retrieval comparison; most other retrieval baselines move to Table 12. The full-pool table also changes its BERT label to Legal-BERT while retaining identical scores, leaving that comparator's identity unresolved.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include a 300-case pilot with and without a supplied charge list, generation guided by two FET exemplars, additional model configurations, and collaboration using ten factual keywords with expert validation. The original disambiguation sample, retrieval pools, and evaluation metrics are retained; these are added protocols rather than established reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands analyses of dependence on the generating model, downstream backbone, exemplar guidance, combined knowledge sources, and human collaboration. It also adds a misappropriation failure example and charge-list sensitivity analysis. The original FET-only retrieval ablation and embezzlement case study remain.

E5.justification: V2 introduces paired McNemar tests comparing four LLM-generated FET configurations against expert FETs across three disambiguation groups, reporting twelve p-values in Table 11. V1 contains no corresponding significance analysis. This adds statistical support without establishing an increase in repeated runs or newly specified seed counts.

E6.justification: Original GPT-4o results and full-pool retrieval values are retained, but substantial new results appear. Examples include ICL disambiguation accuracy/F1 of 92.69/93.00, collaborative annotations at 92.84/93.04, and Qwen retrieval MRR of 0.2168 without versus 0.2206 with expert guidance. Appendix D adds pilot findings, while GEAR's results are removed. The introduction's percentage gains are equivalent relative expressions of the retained Table 3 differences.

T1.justification: No new mathematical definitions, theoretical results, or proofs appear. V1's cosine-similarity and weighted-combination equations are expressed procedurally in v2 Section 8.2 with the same underlying calculation.

C1.justification: The central knowledge-base contribution and claim that expert knowledge benefits legal reasoning remain. V2 explicitly broadens its claimed consistency across prompting strategies and model types, and its conclusion adds potential applications in other areas requiring expert judgment.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of failures to recognize when legal interpretation is necessary, weak discrimination from frequent factual keywords, and information lost when retrieval excludes original case facts. Sections 9 and 12 discuss collaboration shortcomings, annotation costs, and coarse factual–legal integration, substantially extending v1's mainly jurisdictional limitation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies previously missing charge-level generation, charge-prediction, and case-generation prompts in Tables 6, 13, and 14. It also identifies five dataset annotators, CAIL2018-based charge-selection criteria, the 8192-token generation limit, and component model identities. These substantially improve documentation without establishing changes to the underlying retained experiments.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially toward legal LLMs and their reasoning limitations, adding works including Lawyer LLaMA, DiSC-LawLLM, LegalBench, LegalDiscourse, LawBench, and LexEval. Earlier discussion and citations concerning debates between competing crime-constitution theories are condensed or removed, while additional legal-interpretation scholarship supports the revised framing.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, annotation explanations, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. V2 separates Background from Related Work, introduces an early analysis of LLM failures, integrates data statistics into dataset construction, and adds a Discussion section. This substantially reorganizes the argument beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: V2 adds a failure-example figure, revises the hierarchy diagram, and removes the retrieval workflow diagram. It expands and restructures result tables, relocates retrieval baselines to the appendix, and adds collaboration, significance, and prompt tables. The distribution plots and embezzlement case-study display are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens conclusions previously supported mainly by one primary LLM: it tests alternative models and prompting strategies, adds paired significance tests, and documents previously missing generation procedures and charge-selection criteria. Its collaboration analysis and concrete retrieval limitations also improve critical assessment. Removing GEAR narrows one comparison, and the unexplained BERT/Legal-BERT relabeling weakens traceability, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the gains in evidential support, reproducibility, and clarity.
